mainLabels.label: Enemy Image
mainLabels.description: Enemy Image portrays an outgroup as a threatening collective that is fundamentally different or less than human. This can affect the ingroup’s general perception of the outgroup and lead to desensitization, enabling participation in violence without remorse.

subLabels.label: Homogenization
subLabels.description: Homogenization describes how language can make an outgroup appear as one single, uniform group. Individual differences become less visible. As a result, the actions, traits, or perceived threat of some individuals may be projected onto the whole group. This can blur the distinction between civilians and combatants.

subLabels.label: Immutability
subLabels.description: Immutability presents an outgroup as unchangeable in its nature, ideology, or threat. The group seems impossible to reform, live with peacefully, or negotiate with. When a group is seen as a permanent danger, peaceful solutions can seem naive, impossible, or even risky.

subLabels.label: Essentialization
subLabels.description: Essentialization portrays the outgroup as evil, immoral, or fundamentally different from the ingroup. If a group is to be severely harmed, it must not be perceived as similar to the ingroup, because shared similarities foster empathy.

subLabels.label: Dehumanization
subLabels.description: Dehumanization describes language that presents an outgroup as less than fully human. This can happen when people are compared to animals, pests, diseases, objects, or described as inferior. For example, they may be called “vermin” or described as a “disease.” Their suffering may then seem less important or less real. Violence against them can appear less disturbing, more acceptable, or easier to justify. In this way, dehumanization can help mobilize the ingroup by reducing moral hesitation.

subLabels.label: Threat Depiction
subLabels.description: Threat Depiction describes how language can present an outgroup as a threat to the ingroup, its safety, values, territory, or future. The threat is often linked to a demanded action or measure. This can make certain responses appear necessary, protective, or justified. Once an outgroup is framed as dangerous, people may interpret later information through this threat image. Details that confirm the threat can seem more believable, while contradicting information may receive less attention.

mainLabels.label: Just Cause
mainLabels.description: Just Cause frames violent or harmful measures as rational, necessary, or morally justified. By linking a measure to a specific cause, these patterns create a logic of justification in which violence can appear legitimate rather than arbitrary.

subLabels.label: Security Rationale
subLabels.description: Security Rationale describes how language can present violent, harmful, or controlling measures as necessary for the security and protection of the ingroup. The focus is not mainly on depicting a threat, but on using security as a reason for action. In this way, such measures can appear reasonable, defensive, or legitimate.

subLabels.label: Self-Defense / Counter-Terrorism
subLabels.description: Self-Defense / Counter-Terrorism describes how language can justify violent or harmful measures by framing them as self-defense or counter-terrorism. The focus is not on depicting a threat alone, but on how this threat is used to justify a concrete action. As a result, the measure can appear legitimate, necessary or even defensive.

subLabels.label: Retaliation
subLabels.description: Retaliation presents harmful measures as revenge, a necessary reaction, or punishment for past suffering and harm caused by an outgroup.

mainLabels.label: Individual Needs
mainLabels.description: Individual Needs appeals to the ingroup’s personal needs. By making people feel needed, respected, hopeful, or part of a meaningful project, these patterns can encourage support and participation.

subLabels.label: Meaning
subLabels.description: Meaning frames actions, policies, or sacrifices as part of a larger meaning making cause. It elevates their importance by linking them to historical, religious, or national stories, presenting them as important for the community or the nation.

subLabels.label: Status
subLabels.description: Status describes statements that emphasize strength, rank, recognition, or national self-assertion.

subLabels.label: Hope for Victory
subLabels.description: Hope for Victory describes how language can make victory or success seem possible and close. This can give the ingroup hope, help people keep going, and prevent defeatism.

mainLabels.label: Rhetorical Foreclosure
mainLabels.description: Rhetorical Foreclosure narrows the ingroup’s perspective by dismissing alternatives, criticism, and moral concerns. In conflict situations, this can be effective because people might question information less critically and place more trust in authorities.

subLabels.label: No Alternatives
subLabels.description: No Alternatives presents a measure as unavoidable. By suggesting that there is “no choice” or “no other way,” it dismisses alternatives and frames the action as a necessity rather than a debatable choice.

subLabels.label: Humanity as Weakness
subLabels.description: Humanity as Weakness describes statements that present humanity, mercy, empathy, or restraint as weak, insufficient, or irresponsible. This pattern devalues compassion and makes harshness appear more appropriate or necessary than humanity.

subLabels.label: External Criticism Rejection
subLabels.description: External Criticism Rejection describes statements that dismiss outside criticism as illegitimate, hostile, or antisemitic. This can make external pressure or moral objections appear invalid and protect the ingroup from outside influence.
